strategies.title: Cost Segregation
strategies.shortDescription: Accelerate depreciation on rental properties to reduce taxable income
strategies.fullDescription: Cost segregation is a tax strategy that allows real estate investors to accelerate depreciation deductions by reclassifying components of a building into shorter depreciation periods. Instead of depreciating the entire property over 27.5 or 39 years, certain components like carpeting, appliances, and landscaping can be depreciated over 5, 7, or 15 years.
strategies.bestFor: Properties worth $500K+ purchased or renovated recently

faqs.question: What is cost segregation?
faqs.answer: Cost segregation is a tax planning strategy that identifies and reclassifies personal property assets to shorten depreciation time, resulting in substantial tax savings through accelerated depreciation deductions.

faqs.question: Who benefits most from cost segregation?
faqs.answer: Real estate investors with properties worth $500,000 or more benefit most, especially those who purchased, constructed, or renovated properties in the last 10-15 years.

faqs.question: How much does a cost segregation study cost?
faqs.answer: A typical cost segregation study costs between $5,000 and $15,000, depending on property size and complexity. The tax savings usually far exceed the study cost.

strategies.title: Bonus Depreciation
strategies.shortDescription: Deduct 100 percent of qualifying property cost in the first year
strategies.fullDescription: Bonus depreciation lets you deduct qualifying property in the year it is placed in service instead of spreading it over the recovery period. For 2026 the rate is 100 percent for qualified property acquired after January 19, 2025, made permanent by the 2025 tax law in Section 168(k). Property under a binding contract on or before January 19, 2025 stays on the old phase-down and gets 20 percent in 2026.
strategies.potentialSavings: 100% of qualifying asset cost as a first-year deduction
strategies.bestFor: Equipment, vehicles, and the short-life components a cost segregation study finds

faqs.question: What is the bonus depreciation rate for 2026?
faqs.answer: One hundred percent for qualified property acquired after January 19, 2025 and placed in service in 2026. The 2025 tax law set that rate permanently in Section 168(k). Property under a written binding contract on or before January 19, 2025 stays on the old phase-down and gets 20 percent in 2026.

faqs.question: What qualifies for bonus depreciation?
faqs.answer: New and used tangible property with a recovery period of 20 years or less, off-the-shelf software, and qualified improvement property. The building shell does not qualify, because it runs 27.5 or 39 years.

faqs.question: Can bonus depreciation create a loss?
faqs.answer: Yes. It can create or increase a net operating loss. Whether you can use that loss this year depends on the passive activity rules and the excess business loss cap in Section 461(l).

strategies.title: 1031 Exchange
strategies.shortDescription: Defer capital gains taxes by reinvesting proceeds into like-kind property
strategies.fullDescription: A 1031 exchange, named after Section 1031 of the IRS code, allows real estate investors to defer paying capital gains taxes when they sell an investment property and reinvest the proceeds into another 'like-kind' property. This powerful strategy lets investors grow their portfolio tax-free as long as they continue exchanging properties.
strategies.bestFor: Investors looking to upgrade or diversify their real estate portfolio

faqs.question: What is the 45-day rule in a 1031 exchange?
faqs.answer: You must identify potential replacement properties within 45 days of selling your original property. You can identify up to three properties regardless of value, or more properties if their total value doesn't exceed 200% of the sold property.

faqs.question: What is the 180-day rule in a 1031 exchange?
faqs.answer: You must close on the replacement property within 180 days of selling the original property, or by your tax return due date (including extensions), whichever comes first.

faqs.question: Can you do a 1031 exchange on your primary residence?
faqs.answer: No, 1031 exchanges only apply to investment or business property. However, you can convert a primary residence to a rental property and then do a 1031 exchange after holding it as an investment.

strategies.title: Real Estate Professional Status (REPS)
strategies.shortDescription: Unlock unlimited passive loss deductions against ordinary income
strategies.fullDescription: Real Estate Professional Status is an IRS designation that allows qualifying taxpayers to deduct rental real estate losses against their ordinary income without passive activity loss limitations. This can result in significant tax savings for high-income earners who materially participate in their real estate activities.
strategies.potentialSavings: Unlimited passive losses against W-2 income
strategies.bestFor: Those who spend 750+ hours annually in real estate activities
strategies.typicalCost: Included in tax preparation, but requires detailed time tracking

faqs.question: What are the requirements for Real Estate Professional Status?
faqs.answer: You must spend more than 750 hours in real estate activities AND more than half of your total working hours must be in real estate. You must also materially participate in each rental activity.

faqs.question: Can a spouse qualify for REPS?
faqs.answer: Yes, if one spouse qualifies as a real estate professional, both spouses can benefit on a joint return, even if the other spouse has a full-time W-2 job.

faqs.question: How do I prove Real Estate Professional Status?
faqs.answer: Keep detailed contemporaneous time logs documenting your real estate activities. The IRS may audit REPS claims, so thorough documentation is essential.

strategies.title: Short-Term Rental Loophole
strategies.shortDescription: Deduct short-term rental losses against W-2 income without REPS
strategies.fullDescription: A rental whose average period of customer use is seven days or less is not a rental activity under Reg. 1.469-1T(e)(3)(ii)(A). It is treated as a trade or business, so its loss is not passive when you materially participate. That lets the loss offset W-2 income in the same year, without meeting the 750-hour and more-than-half tests for real estate professional status.
strategies.bestFor: W-2 earners who run the bookings themselves in a short-stay market
strategies.typicalCost: Included in tax preparation with STR experience

faqs.question: What is the 7-day rule for short-term rentals?
faqs.answer: If the average period of customer use is seven days or less, the activity is not a rental activity under the passive loss rules. Average stay is total rental days divided by the number of separate guest stays in the tax year.

faqs.question: What counts as material participation for a short-term rental?
faqs.answer: You need to pass one of the seven tests in Temp. Reg. 1.469-5T(a). The usual one is more than 100 hours during the year with no other individual working more hours than you. Your spouse hours count as yours.

faqs.question: What happens to the savings when I sell?
faqs.answer: Depreciation reduces your basis, so it comes back as gain on sale. The building share is unrecaptured Section 1250 gain at up to 25 percent and the cost segregation components are mostly Section 1245 recapture at ordinary rates.

strategies.title: Section 179 Deduction
strategies.shortDescription: Immediately expense up to $1.16M in business equipment
strategies.fullDescription: Section 179 allows businesses to deduct the full purchase price of qualifying equipment and software purchased during the tax year, rather than depreciating it over time. The deduction limit and phase-out threshold are updated by the IRS each year.
strategies.bestFor: Businesses purchasing equipment, vehicles, or software

faqs.question: What is the current Section 179 limit?
faqs.answer: Section 179 limits and phase-out thresholds change by tax year. Check the current IRS numbers before you rely on any model or equipment plan.

faqs.question: What qualifies for Section 179?
faqs.answer: Qualifying property includes tangible personal property, off-the-shelf software, qualified improvement property, and certain vehicles used for business.

faqs.question: Can Section 179 create a loss?
faqs.answer: No, Section 179 cannot create or increase a net operating loss. The deduction is limited to your taxable business income. However, you can use bonus depreciation for amounts exceeding this limit.

strategies.title: Self-Directed IRA
strategies.shortDescription: Invest retirement funds in real estate, businesses, and alternative assets
strategies.fullDescription: A Self-Directed IRA allows you to invest your retirement funds in a wider range of assets beyond stocks and bonds, including real estate, private businesses, precious metals, and more. All income and gains grow tax-deferred (Traditional) or tax-free (Roth).
strategies.potentialSavings: Tax-deferred or tax-free growth on investments
strategies.bestFor: Investors who want to diversify retirement funds into real estate

faqs.question: What can I invest in with a Self-Directed IRA?
faqs.answer: You can invest in real estate, private equity, precious metals, tax liens, promissory notes, and more. Prohibited investments include life insurance, collectibles, and S-corp stock.

faqs.question: Can I buy rental property with my IRA?
faqs.answer: Yes, but all expenses must be paid from the IRA, and all income must return to the IRA. You cannot personally use the property or perform your own repairs.

faqs.question: What are prohibited transactions in a Self-Directed IRA?
faqs.answer: You cannot transact with disqualified persons (yourself, family members, or entities you control), use IRA assets for personal benefit, or receive compensation from IRA investments.

strategies.title: Solo 401(k)
strategies.shortDescription: Contribute up to $69,000 per year as a self-employed individual
strategies.fullDescription: A Solo 401(k), also known as an Individual 401(k), is a retirement plan for self-employed individuals with no full-time employees. It allows significantly higher contribution limits than a traditional IRA, plus the ability to take loans from your account and invest in alternative assets.
strategies.potentialSavings: High annual contribution ceiling with catch-up options

faqs.question: What are the current Solo 401(k) contribution limits?
faqs.answer: Solo 401(k) employee and employer contribution limits are updated by the IRS each year. Confirm the current-year limits before you finalize your contribution plan.

faqs.question: Can I have a Solo 401(k) and a regular 401(k)?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the employee deferral limit is shared across all 401(k) plans. Employer contribution rules are calculated separately for each plan.

faqs.question: Can I take a loan from my Solo 401(k)?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can borrow up to 50% of your account balance or $50,000, whichever is less. This is a key advantage over SEP IRAs which don't allow loans.

strategies.title: HSA Triple Tax Advantage
strategies.shortDescription: The only account with tax-free contributions, growth, AND withdrawals
strategies.fullDescription: A Health Savings Account (HSA) offers a triple tax advantage: contributions are tax-deductible, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free. Many investors use HSAs as stealth retirement accounts by paying current medical expenses out-of-pocket and letting the HSA grow.
strategies.potentialSavings: Triple tax benefit with annual contribution limits
strategies.bestFor: Healthy individuals with high-deductible health plans

faqs.question: What is the triple tax advantage of an HSA?
faqs.answer: HSAs offer: (1) tax-deductible contributions, (2) tax-free growth and investment earnings, and (3) tax-free withdrawals for qualified medical expenses. No other account offers all three.

faqs.question: Can I use my HSA for retirement?
faqs.answer: Yes! After age 65, you can withdraw HSA funds for any purpose. Non-medical withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income (like a traditional IRA), but medical withdrawals remain tax-free.

faqs.question: What is the HSA investment strategy?
faqs.answer: Pay current medical expenses out-of-pocket, save receipts, invest your HSA in index funds, and let it grow tax-free. You can reimburse yourself for those expenses at any time in the future.

strategies.title: Augusta Rule (Section 280A)
strategies.shortDescription: Rent your home to your business tax-free for up to 14 days
strategies.fullDescription: The Augusta Rule allows homeowners to rent their home for up to 14 days per year without reporting the rental income. Business owners can leverage this by having their business rent their personal residence for meetings, retreats, or events at fair market rates.
strategies.bestFor: Business owners who can legitimately use their home for business purposes
strategies.typicalCost: May need appraisal for fair market rent ($200-500)

faqs.question: What is the Augusta Rule?
faqs.answer: Section 280A(g) allows homeowners to rent their home for 14 days or fewer per year without reporting the income. Business owners use this by having their company rent their home for legitimate business events.

faqs.question: How much can I charge under the Augusta Rule?
faqs.answer: You must charge fair market rent based on comparable event venues in your area. Document rates for similar venues to support your pricing.

faqs.question: What documentation do I need?
faqs.answer: Keep minutes of meetings, attendee lists, agendas, photos, and comparable rental rates. The business purpose must be legitimate and documented.

strategies.title: S-Corp Tax Strategy
strategies.shortDescription: Save 15.3% self-employment tax by splitting income into salary and distributions
strategies.fullDescription: An S-Corporation election allows business owners to split their income between a reasonable salary (subject to payroll taxes) and distributions (not subject to self-employment tax). This can result in significant savings on the 15.3% self-employment tax.
strategies.typicalCost: $500 - $2,000/year for payroll and additional tax prep

faqs.question: How much can I save with an S-Corp?
faqs.answer: If your business profits $100,000 and you pay yourself $50,000 in salary, you save self-employment tax on the $50,000 distribution, approximately $7,650.

faqs.question: What is a reasonable salary for an S-Corp?
faqs.answer: A reasonable salary is what you'd pay someone to do your job in the open market. Consider industry norms, your experience, location, and time spent. Too low invites IRS scrutiny.

faqs.question: When does an S-Corp make sense?
faqs.answer: Generally when business profits exceed $50,000-$60,000 annually. Below this, the administrative costs may outweigh the tax savings.

strategies.title: Opportunity Zone Investing
strategies.shortDescription: Defer and reduce capital gains by investing in designated communities
strategies.fullDescription: Qualified Opportunity Zones allow investors to defer capital gains taxes by reinvesting gains into designated low-income communities. Hold for 10+ years and pay zero tax on appreciation of the Opportunity Zone investment itself.
strategies.potentialSavings: 100% exclusion on OZ gains after 10 years
strategies.bestFor: Long-term investors with significant capital gains to reinvest
strategies.typicalCost: Fund fees vary; direct investment requires significant capital

faqs.question: How do Opportunity Zones work?
faqs.answer: Invest capital gains into a Qualified Opportunity Fund within 180 days. Defer the original gain until 2026 (or sale). If held 10+ years, pay zero tax on OZ investment appreciation.

faqs.question: What qualifies as an Opportunity Zone investment?
faqs.answer: Must invest through a Qualified Opportunity Fund (QOF) that holds at least 90% of assets in qualified opportunity zone property, including real estate and operating businesses.

faqs.question: Is the original capital gain eliminated?
faqs.answer: No, the original gain is deferred until December 31, 2026 (or earlier sale). However, appreciation on the OZ investment is tax-free if held 10+ years.

personas.title: W-2 Employees
personas.description: Tax strategies for salaried workers looking to reduce their tax burden
personas.metaDescription: What a salaried worker can actually do about taxes, grouped by whether the move needs nothing, a rental, or a spouse or side business.
personas.answer: Most of what a W-2 earner can do happens inside payroll and investment accounts. Fill the 401k and the HSA, use any after-tax 401k room, add a backdoor Roth IRA, then harvest losses and time charitable gifts. Everything larger than that needs a rental, a side business, or a spouse with time.
personas.lede: A paycheck is the hardest income to shelter. There is no entity to route it through, and unreimbursed employee expenses are not deductible on a federal return. So the moves below are grouped by what each one asks of you.

groups.heading: No business needed
groups.intro: These work with nothing but your own payroll elections and a brokerage account. Start here, because they are the only moves that are fully under your control.

groups.heading: Needs a rental
groups.intro: These only exist if you own property. They can be the largest numbers on the page, and they carry the most work, the most records, and depreciation recapture when you sell.

groups.heading: Needs a spouse or a side business
groups.intro: These need income or hours that a full-time job leaves no room for. On a joint return a spouse can meet tests you cannot.

faqs.question: I max my 401k and HSA. What is left?
faqs.answer: After-tax 401k room converted to Roth, a backdoor Roth IRA, a dependent care FSA, tax-loss harvesting in a taxable account, and charitable bunching through a donor-advised fund. Those five need no business, no property, and no spouse. Anything larger than that does.

faqs.question: What tax strategies are available to W-2 employees?
faqs.answer: A health savings account, after-tax 401k contributions converted to Roth, a backdoor Roth IRA above the income limits, a dependent care FSA, bunching itemized deductions into alternate years, and the short-term rental loophole if a rental property is part of the plan.

faqs.question: Can I deduct expenses against my wages?
faqs.answer: Almost never. Unreimbursed employee business expenses are not deductible on a federal return. Pre-tax payroll items such as the 401k, the HSA, health premiums, and the dependent care FSA are the main way to lower wages before they reach the return.

faqs.question: How can W-2 employees deduct rental property losses?
faqs.answer: The short-term rental loophole treats a rental with an average stay of seven days or less as non-passive when you materially participate, which takes it outside the passive activity loss limits that normally block the deduction. Clearing the seven-day test is only the first half. Material participation is a separate test with its own hour requirements and its own record keeping.

faqs.question: Can I qualify for real estate professional status with a full-time job?
faqs.answer: No. The test needs more than 750 hours and more than half of your working time in real property trades or businesses, and a full-time job makes the second half impossible. A spouse who is not working full time elsewhere is the realistic route on a joint return.

faqs.question: Does an LLC lower the tax on my salary?
faqs.answer: No. An LLC does not change how wages are taxed. Entity choice starts to matter only once you have self-employment or rental income, and even then the S-corp question depends on profit level, payroll cost, and state treatment.

personas.title: Physicians
personas.description: Tax strategies for employed and moonlighting physicians, grouped by whether the move needs only payroll, a 1099 income stream, or a spouse with time
personas.metaDescription: What a physician can do about a top-bracket W-2: 403(b), 457(b), HSA and backdoor Roth first, then solo 401(k) or S-corp on 1099 pay, then rentals via a spouse.
personas.answer: For most physicians the best tax strategy is the plain one: fill every pre-tax account the employer offers, including a 457(b) if the hospital is a nonprofit, add an HSA and a backdoor Roth, and stop there unless there is other income. Moonlighting or locums pay unlocks a solo 401(k) and possibly an S-corp. Rental losses that offset physician wages usually need a spouse who can meet the participation tests, not the physician.
personas.lede: A physician’s income is mostly W-2, mostly taxed at the top rates, and the specified service rules take away the deductions a business owner would lean on. So the moves below are grouped by the facts that unlock them: payroll alone, a 1099 income stream, a spouse with time, or a single high-income year.

groups.heading: Employed W-2 physician
groups.intro: Hospital and health-system physicians get the same short list as any W-2 earner, with one addition. Many nonprofit employers offer a 457(b) next to the 403(b), and the two have separate deferral limits, so both can be filled in the same year. Read the plan document first if it is a non-governmental 457(b): the balance stays an asset of the employer until it is paid out, and the payout schedule is fixed when you separate. If the plan accepts after-tax contributions and allows in-plan conversion, the mega backdoor Roth is the largest remaining account move. Pre-tax deferrals also lower the adjusted gross income that sets an income-driven student loan payment, which matters if you are counting on PSLF, and a Roth conversion or a joint return does the reverse.

groups.heading: 1099 moonlighting or locums income
groups.intro: Any self-employment income opens a second set of moves. A solo 401(k) takes both an employee deferral and an employer contribution, but the employee deferral limit is shared across every plan you contribute to in the year, so a physician already deferring the maximum through a hospital 403(b) mostly gets the employer side. An S-corp is a payroll-tax question: if hospital wages already exceed the Social Security wage base, the 1099 income only owes the Medicare portion of self-employment tax, so the S-corp saves a few percent of the distribution share and has to beat its own payroll, filing, and state costs. Medicine is a specified service trade or business, so the qualified business income deduction phases out above the income thresholds, and most full-time attendings are above them. A home office deduction is available for the administrative side of a 1099 practice if the space is used exclusively for it, and quarterly estimates keep the 1099 income from producing a penalty in April.

groups.heading: Physician household with a spouse who has time
groups.intro: The largest deductions on this page are rental losses used against physician wages, and a full-time physician almost never qualifies for them alone. Real estate professional status needs more than 750 hours and more than half of working time in real property trades, which a clinical schedule rules out; on a joint return, a spouse who is not working full time elsewhere can meet the test for the household. The short-term rental loophole has a lower bar, material participation without the 750-hour test, and either spouse’s hours count toward it. Cost segregation and bonus depreciation are what make the loss large enough to matter in the first year. Depreciation recapture on sale and the hour log are the price.

groups.heading: A high-income year: charitable and timing moves
groups.intro: A signing bonus, a partnership buy-in year, or a large Roth conversion pushes taxable income deeper into the top bracket, and that is the year a deduction is worth the most. A donor-advised fund takes the full deduction now and grants the money out over years. Bunching two or three years of gifts into one return clears the standard deduction that a single year’s gifts may not. Appreciated stock given directly, rather than sold and then donated, skips the capital gain as well as earning the deduction.

faqs.question: What is the best tax strategy for physicians?
faqs.answer: Fill every pre-tax account the employer offers, including a 457(b) where a nonprofit hospital has one, then add an HSA and a backdoor Roth IRA. That list is fully under your control and needs no business. Moonlighting or locums income adds a solo 401(k) and an S-corp analysis. Rental losses against physician wages, the largest numbers, usually need a spouse who can meet the participation tests.

faqs.question: Do physicians qualify for the QBI deduction?
faqs.answer: Only on self-employment or practice income, and only when taxable income is below the thresholds. Medicine is a specified service trade or business, so the qualified business income deduction phases out above the income thresholds and then disappears. An employed physician with no 1099 income has no qualified business income at all.

faqs.question: Can a physician with a full-time hospital job use the short-term rental loophole?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you or your spouse materially participate in the rental and the average guest stay is seven days or less. The loophole does not need the 750-hour real estate professional test, which is what makes it reachable on a clinical schedule. Material participation still has its own hour requirements, usually 100 hours and more than anyone else, and it needs a contemporaneous log.

faqs.question: Should a moonlighting physician form an S-corp?
faqs.answer: Only after modeling it. If hospital wages already exceed the Social Security wage base, the 1099 income owes only the Medicare portion of self-employment tax, so the S-corp saves a few percent of the distribution share and must cover its own payroll, filing, and state costs. It usually starts to make sense when the 1099 income is large and steady, not in the first year of occasional shifts.

faqs.question: Is a 457(b) separate from a 403(b) limit?
faqs.answer: Yes. A 457(b) has its own deferral limit, separate from the shared 401(k) and 403(b) limit, so a physician at a nonprofit hospital that offers both can defer into both in the same year. The caveat is that a non-governmental 457(b) stays an unsecured asset of the employer until it is paid out, and the distribution schedule is set when you leave, so read the plan document before relying on it.

personas.title: Dentists
personas.description: Tax strategies for associate dentists and practice owners, from payroll accounts through the practice entity, the building, and the sale
personas.metaDescription: Tax strategies for dentists at each stage: associate payroll and 1099 moves, owner S-corp salary and cash balance plans, the building, and the practice sale.
personas.answer: For an associate, the best tax strategy is the account list: the practice 401(k), an HSA, a backdoor Roth, and a solo 401(k) if the pay is 1099. For a practice owner, the two largest levers are a reasonable S-corp salary paired with a cash balance or defined benefit plan, and depreciation on equipment and the building. At exit, how the sale is structured decides the tax more than any deduction in the years before it.
personas.lede: Dentistry is a specified service business with heavy equipment, often a building, and usually a sale at the end. That makes the tax picture different from a physician’s: less can be done inside payroll and far more inside the practice entity. The moves below follow the career, from associate to owner to seller.

groups.heading: Associate dentist (W-2 or 1099)
groups.intro: A W-2 associate has the same list as any employee: fill the practice’s 401(k) if there is one, an HSA if the health plan qualifies, and a backdoor Roth IRA above the income limits. A 1099 associate is self-employed, which opens a solo 401(k) with both employee and employer contributions, plus quarterly estimated payments and the home office and vehicle deductions for the administrative side of the work. The S-corp question at this stage depends on the size of the 1099 income and the state; in the first year it is often premature.

groups.heading: Practice owner
groups.intro: Once you own the practice, the entity and the retirement plan do most of the work. An S-corp splits pay into a reasonable salary and distributions, and reasonable for a producing dentist is benchmarked against what an associate would be paid for the same clinical work, so the distribution share is smaller than owners hope. A cash balance or defined benefit plan layered on top of the 401(k) allows the largest deductible contributions available to a stable, high-income owner, at the cost of required contributions for eligible staff. That staff point is also the catch with a solo 401(k): once the practice has employees, it stops being solo and the plan has to cover them. Section 179 and bonus depreciation cover chairs, imaging, milling units, and other equipment in the year it is placed in service. The Augusta rule rents your home to the practice for up to 14 days of real meetings. Hiring your children for real work moves income into their bracket. The qualified business income deduction phases out for specified service businesses above the income thresholds, so most owners cannot count on it, and a pass-through entity tax election can rescue part of the state tax deduction where the state offers one.

groups.heading: Practice real estate
groups.intro: Many owners buy the building. Holding it in a separate entity and leasing it to the practice is the standard way to keep the building apart from the practice’s liabilities, and it lets the building be sold or kept independently of the practice at exit. Cost segregation on a dental build-out is productive because so much of the cost sits in finishes, plumbing, and equipment-specific systems with short recovery lives. The catch is the self-rental rule: net rental income from a property leased to a business in which you materially participate is treated as non-passive, so it cannot absorb passive losses from other rentals, while a net loss from the building stays passive. The depreciation still lowers the rent that is taxed; it does not create a loss you can use against practice income.

groups.heading: Selling the practice
groups.intro: The exit is usually the largest taxable event of a dental career, and the structure decides the rate. Purchase price allocation splits the sale among goodwill, equipment, and covenants, and each piece is taxed differently: goodwill at capital gains rates, equipment depreciation at ordinary recapture rates. An installment sale spreads the gain across the years payments are received, which can keep part of it under the top bracket and the net investment income tax threshold, at the cost of collection risk on the buyer. A charitable remainder trust converts part of an appreciated practice or building into lifetime income with a current deduction. If the building is sold separately, a 1031 exchange can defer that gain into another property.

Installment sale vs deferred sales trust for a practice exit

faqs.question: What is the best tax strategy for dentists?
faqs.answer: It depends on the stage. An associate should fill the practice 401(k), an HSA, and a backdoor Roth, and open a solo 401(k) if paid on a 1099. A practice owner gets the most from an S-corp with a defensible salary, a cash balance plan stacked on the 401(k), and Section 179 or bonus depreciation on equipment. An owner who also holds the building adds cost segregation. At exit, the sale structure matters more than any single deduction.

faqs.question: Do dentists qualify for QBI?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. Dentistry is a specified service trade or business, so the qualified business income deduction is full below the income thresholds, phases out through a range above them, and is gone past it. An associate with modest 1099 income may qualify; a producing owner usually does not. Because the test is on taxable income, a large retirement plan contribution can pull some owners back under the thresholds in a given year.

faqs.question: How much salary does a dentist S-corp have to pay?
faqs.answer: Enough to be reasonable for the clinical work you do, which is benchmarked against what an associate would be paid to produce the same dentistry. A producing owner therefore has a high reasonable salary and a smaller distribution share than a non-producing owner would. The saving is the payroll tax on distributions, and above the Social Security wage base only the Medicare portion of that tax remains.

faqs.question: Can a dentist deduct the practice building?
faqs.answer: Through depreciation, and often faster through a cost segregation study, because a dental build-out is heavy in short-life components. If you own the building in a separate entity and lease it to your practice, the self-rental rule treats the net rental income as non-passive, so the building’s depreciation lowers the taxed rent but a net loss cannot offset practice income or absorb other passive losses.

faqs.question: Is a cash balance plan worth it for a dental practice?
faqs.answer: It is the largest deductible contribution available to a stable, high-income owner, and it stacks on top of a 401(k). The trade is that it is a defined benefit plan: contributions are required each year, eligible staff must be covered, and it needs an actuary. It fits an owner with several years of consistent profit who wants to shelter a large amount before an exit, and it does not fit a practice with volatile income.

personas.title: W-2 Executives
personas.description: Tax strategies for executives and senior employees in the 37% bracket with equity compensation and no business to route pay through
personas.metaDescription: What a 37%-bracket executive can do: 401(k) and after-tax room, backdoor Roth, HSA, equity and deferred comp timing, and what does not work for pure W-2 pay.
personas.answer: For an executive in the 37% bracket, the best tax strategy is to fill every account the employer offers, including after-tax 401(k) room converted to Roth, add a backdoor Roth and an HSA, then manage the timing of equity compensation and charitable gifts. Deferred compensation can move income to a lower-bracket year but ties it to the employer’s solvency. The large deductions, rental losses used against wages, need a spouse who can meet the participation tests or hours you probably do not have.
personas.lede: At $300,000 or more of W-2 pay, most of the advice written for business owners does not apply. There is no entity to route salary through, unreimbursed employee expenses are not deductible, and a good share of the income arrives as equity you did not choose the timing of. The moves below are grouped by what each one asks of you, ending with what does not work.

groups.heading: Payroll and account moves
groups.intro: Start with what the plan document allows. Beyond the pre-tax deferral, some employer plans accept after-tax contributions and permit in-plan Roth conversion, which is the mega backdoor Roth and the largest remaining account move for a high earner. A backdoor Roth IRA works above the income limits as long as you hold no pre-tax IRA balances that trigger the pro-rata rule. An HSA needs a qualifying high-deductible plan and is the only account that escapes tax on the way in, during growth, and on the way out for medical costs. A dependent care FSA is small but costs nothing. If the 401(k) holds appreciated employer stock, net unrealized appreciation can move that growth to capital gains rates at separation.

groups.heading: Equity compensation and deferred pay
groups.intro: RSUs are taxed as wages when they vest, and the default withholding on a vest is often below the 37% rate, so the first job is to fix the underpayment before it becomes a penalty. Selling at vest costs nothing extra in tax and removes the concentration; holding starts the clock on long-term capital gains for the growth after vest. NSOs are wages at exercise on the spread. ISOs are not, but the spread is an alternative minimum tax preference item, so a large exercise needs an AMT projection first, and the holding periods for a qualifying disposition decide whether the gain is capital or ordinary. ESPP discounts are ordinary income, and the holding period changes how much of the rest is capital gain. Non-qualified deferred compensation pushes salary or bonus into later years, which helps if those years are lower-bracket; the trade is that the deferred amount is an unsecured claim on the employer, the election is made before the year the pay is earned, and the payout schedule is locked when you elect. A concentrated position in a taxable account is also where tax-loss harvesting and direct gifts of appreciated shares do the most work, and if the employer was a qualifying small C corporation when the shares were issued, Section 1202 may exclude part of the gain after five years.

groups.heading: Rental losses against wages
groups.intro: This is where the large numbers are and where most executives are disqualified. Rental losses are passive, and passive losses cannot offset wages unless one of two exceptions applies. Real estate professional status needs more than 750 hours and more than half of your working time in real property trades, which a full-time role rules out; on a joint return a spouse who is not employed full time elsewhere can meet it. The short-term rental loophole drops the 750-hour test and asks only for material participation in a rental with average stays of seven days or less, usually 100 hours and more than anyone else, and either spouse’s hours count. Cost segregation and bonus depreciation are what make the first-year loss large. Recapture when you sell, and the log, are the cost.

groups.heading: What does not work for a pure W-2
groups.intro: Forming an LLC does not change how wages are taxed; entity choice starts to matter only when there is self-employment or rental income to run through it. Unreimbursed employee expenses, a home office for a remote role, and professional dues are not deductible on a federal return for an employee, even when the employer requires the expense; an accountable-plan reimbursement from the employer is the fix. The qualified business income deduction is for pass-through business income, not salary. Section 179, the Augusta rule, and hiring your children all need a business with real activity, not a title. Changing state residency is a real move only if you actually move, with the day counts and domicile evidence to prove it; a second home in a no-tax state does not do it on its own. Everything that does work for a pure W-2 earner is in the first group.

faqs.question: What is the best tax strategy for a W-2 executive in the 37% bracket?
faqs.answer: Fill every account the employer offers: the pre-tax 401(k), any after-tax 401(k) room converted to Roth, an HSA, and a backdoor Roth IRA. Then manage what you control about equity: withholding at vest, when to sell, and giving appreciated shares instead of cash. Deferred compensation and rental losses against wages are the two larger moves, and each has a condition most executives cannot meet without a spouse or a real change in circumstances.

faqs.question: Can a W-2 executive use the short-term rental loophole?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you or your spouse materially participate in a rental with an average guest stay of seven days or less. There is no 750-hour test, which is what makes it reachable next to a full-time role, but material participation still means roughly 100 hours and more than anyone else, with a log to prove it. If a manager does more of the work than you do, you fail the test.

faqs.question: How are RSUs taxed, and can I reduce the tax?
faqs.answer: RSUs are ordinary wages at vest, taxed at your marginal rate, and there is no election that changes that. What you control is withholding, so the vest does not create an underpayment penalty, and what happens after vest: sell at once to remove the concentration at no extra tax cost, or hold to start the long-term capital gains clock on the growth. Shares held over a year can be given to a donor-advised fund for a deduction at fair value with no gain recognized.

faqs.question: Is deferred compensation worth it for an executive?
faqs.answer: It depends on the bracket you expect in the payout years and on the employer. Deferring bonus from a 37% year into retirement years taxed lower is a real saving. The deferred amount is an unsecured claim on the company until it is paid, the election has to be made before the year the pay is earned, and the payout schedule cannot easily be changed, so size it to what you could afford to lose if the employer failed.

faqs.question: Can I deduct a home office or work expenses as an employee?
faqs.answer: Not on a federal return. Unreimbursed employee business expenses, including a home office for a remote role, are not deductible for employees. Ask the employer for an accountable-plan reimbursement instead, which is tax-free to you and deductible to them. A home office deduction only exists for self-employment income.

catalog.title: Cost segregation
catalog.summary: Reclassifies building components into shorter depreciation lives so deductions land in the early years.

catalog.title: Bonus depreciation
catalog.summary: Deducts a large share of qualifying property costs in the first year instead of over its useful life.

catalog.title: Rental property depreciation
catalog.summary: Deducts a rental building over 27.5 years and tracks the basis that matters at sale.

catalog.title: Real estate professional status
catalog.summary: Removes the passive loss limit so rental losses can offset ordinary income.

catalog.title: REPS vs the STR loophole
catalog.summary: The 750-hour and more-than-half tests next to the seven-day average and the 100-hour test, and which one a W-2 earner can meet.

catalog.title: Short-term rental loophole
catalog.summary: Deducts short-term rental losses against W-2 income when average stays are seven days or less and you materially participate.

catalog.title: Depreciation recapture on a short-term rental
catalog.summary: What the loophole costs on the day you sell: Section 1250 gain at up to 25 percent and Section 1245 recapture at ordinary rates.

catalog.title: 1031 exchange
catalog.summary: Defers capital gains tax when sale proceeds are reinvested in like-kind property.

catalog.title: Installment sale
catalog.summary: Spreads the gain on a sale across the years the payments are actually received.

catalog.title: Opportunity zone investing
catalog.summary: Defers and reduces capital gains reinvested in designated communities.

catalog.title: Qualified opportunity zone funds
catalog.summary: Holds opportunity zone investments through a fund that has to meet asset and improvement tests.

catalog.title: Primary residence gain exclusion
catalog.summary: Excludes up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 filing jointly, on the sale of a main home under Section 121.

catalog.title: S-corp election
catalog.summary: Splits owner pay between salary and distributions to cut self-employment tax.

catalog.title: Qualified business income deduction
catalog.summary: Deducts up to 20% of qualified pass-through business income.

catalog.title: Section 179 expensing
catalog.summary: Expenses qualifying equipment in the year it is placed in service instead of depreciating it.

catalog.title: Business vehicle deduction
catalog.summary: Deducts vehicle costs through Section 179, standard mileage, or the actual expense method.

catalog.title: Home office deduction
catalog.summary: Deducts the business-use share of your home under the simplified or actual expense method.

catalog.title: Augusta rule
catalog.summary: Rents your home to your business for up to 14 days a year without reporting the rent as income.

catalog.title: Hiring your children
catalog.summary: Puts family members on payroll for real work, moving income into a lower bracket.

catalog.title: Pass-through entity tax
catalog.summary: Pays state tax at the entity level so the deduction survives the federal SALT cap.

catalog.title: Captive insurance
catalog.summary: Forms a licensed insurance company to cover real business risks and deduct the premiums.

catalog.title: Solo 401(k)
catalog.summary: Combines employee deferrals and employer contributions for an owner-only business.

catalog.title: Health savings account
catalog.summary: Contributions, growth, and qualified medical withdrawals all escape tax.

catalog.title: Dependent care FSA
catalog.summary: Pays childcare and dependent care costs with pre-tax payroll dollars.

catalog.title: Backdoor Roth IRA
catalog.summary: Reaches a Roth IRA through a non-deductible contribution and conversion when income exceeds the Roth limits.

catalog.title: Mega backdoor Roth
catalog.summary: Uses after-tax 401(k) contributions and in-plan conversion to add Roth dollars above the deferral limit.

catalog.title: Roth conversion ladder
catalog.summary: Converts traditional balances in planned yearly slices to control the bracket and open penalty-free access.

catalog.title: Self-directed IRA
catalog.summary: Holds real estate, private companies, and other alternative assets inside a retirement account.

catalog.title: Net unrealized appreciation
catalog.summary: Moves employer stock out of a 401(k) so the appreciation is taxed at capital gains rates.

catalog.title: Tax loss harvesting
catalog.summary: Sells losing positions to offset realized gains while respecting the wash-sale rule.

catalog.title: Tax gain harvesting
catalog.summary: Realizes gains deliberately in a low-income year to reset basis at the 0% or 15% rate.

catalog.title: Qualified small business stock
catalog.summary: Excludes gain on qualifying C corporation stock held five years under Section 1202.

catalog.title: Donor-advised fund
catalog.summary: Takes the charitable deduction in the year the account is funded and grants the money out later.

catalog.title: Charitable remainder trust
catalog.summary: Converts an appreciated asset into lifetime income with a current deduction and deferred gain.

catalog.title: Bunching deductions
catalog.summary: Concentrates two years of charitable gifts and other itemized deductions into one year to clear the standard deduction.

catalog.title: Estimated tax payments
catalog.summary: Times quarterly payments and safe-harbor amounts so you avoid underpayment penalties.

catalog.title: Income shifting
catalog.summary: Moves income to family members or entities taxed at lower rates.

catalog.title: State tax residency
catalog.summary: Establishes domicile and day-count evidence before changing the state that taxes your income.
